value.overview: The Pied-billed Grebe is a small, stocky waterbird found widely across the Americas. It has a short, thick bill, a rounded body, and often swims low in the water. Unlike many waterbirds, it can sink gradually until only the head is visible, helping it escape danger. It is comfortable in quiet freshwater wetlands and is an adaptable species that can use both natural marshes and human-made ponds.
value.classification: The Pied-billed Grebe belongs to the grebe family, Podicipedidae, and the order Podicipediformes. Its scientific name is Podilymbus podiceps.
value.identification: Adults are mostly brown above and paler below, with a compact body, short neck, and small rounded head. The bill is pale with a prominent dark vertical band during the breeding season; this gives the species its common name. Breeding birds may show a black throat and darker facial markings. In nonbreeding plumage, the bill band and throat markings are less distinct. It has no obvious white wing patch in flight and is usually seen swimming or diving.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Canada and the United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is recorded in suitable freshwater wetlands, including ponds, lakes, marshes, reservoirs, and slow-moving waters. It generally favors open water bordered by emergent vegetation, floating plants, or other cover used for nesting and concealment. It may also occur in moderately brackish coastal wetlands when appropriate freshwater habitat is limited.
value.migrationStatus: Pied-billed Grebes in Costa Rica may include resident birds as well as northern migrants that move south when breeding waters freeze. The species is therefore present in Costa Rica throughout at least part of the year, but the timing and proportion of resident versus migrant individuals vary by region and wetland.
value.breeding: Breeding usually occurs on quiet freshwater ponds, lakes, and marshes with abundant emergent vegetation. The pair builds a floating platform or nest anchored to plants, and both adults may participate in incubation and care of the young. Several eggs are commonly laid, and chicks can swim soon after hatching. Adults often carry small young on their backs and feed them aquatic invertebrates and other small prey. Breeding in Costa Rica is possible where wetlands provide stable water levels and suitable vegetation.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes aquatic insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, small fish, tadpoles, frogs, and occasionally plant material. Pied-billed Grebes obtain food mainly by diving from the surface, but they may also seize prey in shallow water or among vegetation. Their broad bill is well suited to grasping relatively large prey. They often forage alone or in pairs and can remain underwater for surprisingly long periods while searching for food.
value.behavior: This grebe is secretive and usually swims quietly through vegetation or open water. When alarmed, it may dive abruptly, sink low in the water, or swim away rather than fly. It is capable of flight but often avoids it unless disturbed or moving between wetlands. Adults give distinctive low, hollow calls and other barking or clucking sounds. During breeding, pairs defend territories and may display with head movements, calls, and close interactions on the water.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered large, but monitoring in parts of North America indicates a declining trend in recent decades. The direction and strength of population change in Costa Rica are not well quantified.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of freshwater wetlands, water pollution, excessive aquatic vegetation removal, altered water levels, and disturbance at nesting sites can reduce local breeding success. Contaminants and eutrophication may also degrade the aquatic food supply and nesting habitat.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect ponds, marshes, lakes, and reservoirs, including vegetated margins used for nesting. Maintain clean water, avoid unnecessary removal of emergent plants, reduce pesticide and nutrient runoff, and limit disturbance near occupied wetlands during the breeding season. Reporting sightings through structured bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of the species in Costa Rica.
